newsitem.title: ITALY: De Benedetti in control, can he stage turnaround?.
newsitem.headline: De Benedetti in control, can he stage turnaround?.

text.p: Italian financier Carlo De Benedetti has shown he is still in the saddle by installing a trusted ally to run Olivetti but analysts wonder whether Italy's famous turnaround specialist can work his old magic.

The appointment on Wednesday night of Roberto Colaninno, who currently runs car components firm Sogefi, as chief executive officer of the ailing information technology group was greeted by a 11.7 percent rise in Olivetti's share price on Thursday.

Analysts said they were in no doubt De Benedetti, who is the biggest shareholder in Olivetti with a 14.5 percent stake, had shown he was firmly in control after the decision to oust Francesco Caio and replace him with Colaninno.

De Benedetti, who turned the tables barely two weeks after he himself was forced to resign from the board after a boardroom clash with Caio, appeared determined to try to weather the storm in the hope that the company can be nursed back to health.
"I don't think he (De Benedetti) was ever away - there was no real change behind scenes," said Michael Pacitti, an analyst at James Capel in London.

"My impression is that it is by no means over for De Benedetti," said a financial commentator in Milan, who asked not to be named. Newspapers had portrayed De Benedetti's exit from the board earlier in the month as a major reverse for him.
But few doubt that De Benedetti faces a titanic struggle to restore Olivetti's fortunes. The company declared a loss of 440 billion lire ($289 million) in the first half

The boardroom convulsions at Olivetti, made worse by the resignation two weeks ago of a top manager who challenged the accuracy of the company's first-half results, triggered a crisis of confidence on the stock exchange.
Olivetti's shares had lost around 40 percent of their value since the beginning of the month before rebounding after the appointment of Colaninno.
Trading volumes in Olivetti stock have shot up in recent weeks prompting some stockbrokers to suspect that one or more anonymous buyers could be amassing shares in the company.
The share price, which closed at 570 lire on Thursday, is less than half its level at the start of the year.
Market analysts say the company could now be vulnerable to a tilt by corporate raiders or even to a bid by De Benedetti to shore up his own position.

What was now less clear was whether De Benedetti could count indefinitely on the full backing of Milan's powerful and secretive merchant bank Mediobanca, a key shareholder in Olivetti and a mover and shaker in Italian corporate politics.

Mediobanca played a major role in orchestrating a 2.26 trillion lire rights issue at the end of last year which was seen as laying the financial groundwork for a recovery in the loss-making group's fortunes which has failed to materialise.

The Milan bank has been closely linked to the thrusting financier since the late 1970s, when De Benedetti turned Olivetti from a failing typewriter maker into a successful personal computer maker in a textbook turnaround.

Olivetti is now engaged in a similar attempt to refocus its business, investing heavily in telecommunications -- seen as the money spinner of the 1990s -- and slimming down its PC business which has steadily drained away cash.
Italy's leading business newspaper, Il Sole 24 Ore, said that Mediobanca had to do all in its power to resolve the crisis at Olivetti, which has not turned a profit since 1990.
Caio, De Benedetti and others are now at the centre of a preliminary judicial investigation focusing on Olivetti's first half results.
"(Mediobanca) must do verything to prevent a ruinous outcome to the crisis for which it would be considered to be partly responsible," said Il Sole. $=1,525
